text:
alex: quick heads-up — I ran an nsys + perf capture against the cpu-side path for batching/kv-cache on the new routing branch. seeing an unexpected CPU hotspot in Python during request coalescing.
mira: can you paste the timeline or flame snippet? which binary did you sample?
alex: captured with `nsys` (cpu sampling on OS threads) and a complementary `perf record -g` for a single worker. timeline shows a ~120ms window where Python spends ~42% in `assemble_batch` + `serialize_request`. attaching short excerpt: 
```
nsys report shows:
- 00:00:00.120 -> 00:00:00.240 : python3 (assemble_batch)
- 00:00:00.240 -> 00:00:00.300 : python3 (serialize_request)
- kernel launches delayed ~10-20us due to batching loop scheduling
```
jonathan: interesting — is this the new heuristic that tries to wait 2ms for more inflight requests? maybe the wait loop is busy-waiting.
alex: I thought the same. the code uses a plain spin + time.sleep fallback. here's the snippet I instrumented: 
```python
start = time.monotonic()
while len(batch) < max_batch and time.monotonic() - start < wait_ms:
    pass  # spin to avoid context switch
# fallback to sleep(0.0001) after X iterations
```
mira: oof, that spin is a red flag for CPU. on high qps it might be fine, but when qps drops you pay full GIL. can you repro with lower QPS?
alex: yes — at low QPS the spin dominates. at high QPS the cost amortizes. perf callgraph shows heavy symbols: `PyEval_EvalFrameEx`, `PyObject_Call`, plus our `assemble_batch`.
sam: could we move the spin into native C and release GIL around the nanosleep? or use futex-based wait (condition variable) to avoid Python overhead?
jonathan: we should also check KV cache lookup pattern. if assemble_batch does per-item lookup in Python dicts with heavy copying we multiply overhead. any chance of moving lookup into C extension or using a compact vectorized path?
alex: KV lookup accounts for ~15% of that window. biggest chunk is the coalescing logic and JSONy serialization we do on the hot path.
mira: two-pronged mitigation: 1) lower spin-to-sleep threshold + use time.sleep with microsecond resolution; 2) replace JSON serialization with msgpack for internal wire format when crossing threads. cheap to flip for a test.
sam: also try converting the batching loop to an async-friendly path using an asyncio condition variable — should avoid GIL thrashing if we yield properly.
jonathan: for instrumentation, please add `py-spy` sampling and a perf-map of Python symbols; that gives clearer frames than nsys sometimes for pure-Python hotspots. also run `perf record -e cycles:u -g -- python worker.py` and `perf report` to get C/Python mixed stacks.
alex: ack. I've got a perf.data from the run — uploading to the traces bucket: https://internal/traces/1719000000/ncpu-batch-perf.data . cc @ci-bot for the CI perf regression check.
ci-bot: perf-check: new sample uploaded. baseline comparison started (1718000000).
mira: timeline comment: kernel launches are queued on the worker thread for ~10-30us after serialize_request returns. could be due to hold on a thread lock; need to check our threadpool handoff.
alex: I instrumented the handoff — lock hold is short (~1-2us) but we have many acquisitions in tight loop. aggregated cost shows.
jonathan: might be worth batching kernel submissions per N requests at the C API boundary — that reduces Python transitions. tradeoff: marginal added latency for small batches.
sam: for a quick experiment, try reducing the default wait_ms from 2ms to 0.5ms and switch internal encoding to msgpack; then run nsys perf and a synthetic QPS sweep (0.5r/s -> 200r/s) to see unit cost.
alex: running that now, will post results in a follow-up message. preliminary: switching to msgpack cut serialize time by ~3x in microbench. lowering spin threshold shaved ~18% CPU in low-QPS test.
mira: sweet. can you also add a delta flamegraph (before/after) and attach both SVGs? even small changes are convincing for the rollout PR.
alex: yes, adding flamegraphs and the perf reports to the trace dir. also adding a tiny patch to avoid allocating intermediate lists in assemble_batch.
jonathan: once we have numbers, let's make a canary rollout on staging with the new heuristic and observe tail latency. add a rollout policy: 10% -> 50% -> 100% with rollback after 95th percentile latency regression > 5ms.
sam: one more note: check mmap/allocator churn in serialization path — Python alloc/free patterns can show up as syscalls in perf and cost us.
alex: good call. I'll run valgrind-massif style heap snapshots and check malloc hotspots.
ci-bot: perf-check: baseline vs new run diff generated: CPU-perf delta = -12.3% (low qps), P95 latency change = +0.4ms.
mira: that looks promising. once you push the PR, tag me and eng-sre. keep the instrumented traces in the trace bucket for at least 30d.
alex: will do. follow-up with SVGs in ~45m. :rocket:
